children: By Celia Bernhardt

An 11-second TikTok video with more than a million views shows a young woman named Ceci examining a lengthy breakup text she has received. "HE IS ENDING OUR RELATIONSHIP OVER THIS??" reads the caption.
"I don't know if I'll ever understand, but OK," Ceci says aloud as an on-screen widget, "Dictating with Aqua Voice," transcribes her reply.

It looks like just another Tiktoker chronicling her breakup for the world to see. But click on the account and you'll see posts of Ceci getting dumped by text repeatedly, each time for different reasons. Every time, she uses the Aqua Voice app.

Ceci Beck-who said she was happily engaged when she posted and is now married-was paid more than $800 to run the secondary account promoting Aqua Voice. She's part of a legion of side hustlers making money through a stealth marketing method called 'UGC,' or user-generated content.

The posts look like everyday TikTok or Instagram fodder, not paid ads. Occasionally, they include hashtags with "ad" or "partner" after the brand name, but usually don't. Though undisclosed ads violate community guidelines on TikTok, Meta Platforms and YouTube-as well as Federal Trade Commission rules-the ecosystem is flourishing on each platform.

That doesn't concern Beck too much, who says she averages $6,000 a month with UGC and makes additional income helping run an online creator academy. Aqua Voice's head of marketing, Austin Zitting, said the app doesn't have any formal disclosure policies.
"I figure if we do anything wrong enough someone will let us know," he said. "Then, we'll probably have to make some."
'New type of labor force'

Conditions are ripe for this fast-growing gig market: AI has fueled a boom in consumer software startups hungry for cheap marketing. And social-media algorithms now drive content more based on users' interest and less according to a creator's follower count. That's boosting the reach of small creators.

"We're trying to carve out this new type of labor force," said Nick Lawton, the chief executive of Sideshift, a UGC creator marketplace that says it has more than one million registered creator accounts. "Take regular everyday people, pay them $20 a video, have them post an extreme amount."

Meanwhile, brands have discovered that viewers often trust relatable, everyday people over influencers with huge followings. As a Sideshift ad says: "Don't hire an influencer. Hire an army of influencers." Lawton said it advises creators to be aware of and follow all applicable disclosure requirements.
Creators say UGC is one of the few flexible ways to make decent money for the hours they work.

Brooks Langford hasn't been able to find a job in his field since graduating from college last year. He splits his time between barista shifts and UGC campaigns: about five hours of the latter a week earns him between $1,000 and $2,000 each month, he said.

Langford typically balances two or three TikTok and Instagram accounts at once-one for each brand. Companies usually send him weekly briefings with assigned scripts, visual "hooks" to grab viewers' attention, and captions.
Langford said it's typical for UGC posts not to include any disclosure. "I guess easy cash outweighs the slight dishonesty I feel," he said.
Some make more. Caryl Pagulayan, who works with tech startups, earned $11,000 in July after several of her videos went viral. She worked five to seven hours each week.
She first saw UGC as a steppingstone to a full-time marketing job, but is now reconsidering. "I don't have to work much, and these numbers are possible," she said.

Many UGC clients are tiny startups. Some accounts also have promoted more established brands, including human-resources company Deel, AI-powered writing assistant Grammarly, prediction market Kalshi and Brex, a fintech firm. Misleading videos of students winning fake Polymarket bets, as reported by The Wall Street Journal, were also organized as a UGC campaign.

A Kalshi spokeswoman said it was reviewing its relationships with accounts that don't follow its disclosure policies. Grammarly said it asks creators to add #GrammarlyPartner or #GrammarlyCreator to indicate their work with the brand and continues to refine its guidelines. Deel declined to comment, and Brex and Polymarket didn't respond to requests for comment.
Some creators say UGC campaign managers-often marketing contractors who are or were creators themselves-have discouraged them from disclosing their ads.

Kassi Meyer, a stay-at-home mother of two in Ohio, recently started UGC to help with household bills. Before posting her first video for Collect, a paid app owned by Canadian software company Ferrix Labs that helps users find and join class-action lawsuits they may be eligible for, she asked whether to mark it as an ad.
"Say it's not," her campaign manager replied with a smiley face in a text reviewed by the Journal. Ferrix Labs didn't respond to requests for comment.
Meyer and her husband are struggling with debt. She worries that if she marked the videos as ads, she wouldn't get paid-so she doesn't. Still, she said, "it feels a little grimy."
Not a regulatory priority

Some UGC creators said they believed the FTC's guidelines provided enough leeway to create the stealth marketing posts. Others pointed to ad disclosures in the bio section of their social-media accounts or to the fact the accounts are technically "brand-owned" assets, according to their contracts.

That doesn't necessarily get them off the hook if they're getting paid for the content, advertising attorneys say. Still, the practice is so widespread and under the radar that many brands decide nondisclosure is within their risk tolerance.

"The FTC takes action from time to time, but they have limited resources," said Rob Freund, an e-commerce and advertising lawyer in California. "It doesn't seem like enforcing ad disclosure requirements on social media is a top priority right now."
The FTC declined to comment.
Some content creators say they have noticed an uptick in comments to posts calling out undisclosed videos.
"I think it will get to a point, just like a lot of social-media tactics, where people are catching on," Pagulayan said.
